summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This conversation is a working session for "The Method 1.6," an ongoing book construction project in Phase 4 of its build cycle (chat 9 of an ongoing series). The person is the author, and Claude operates as builder/implementer under a strict protocol: project knowledge reviewed first, all work in Zeno segmentation (fetch → read → analyse → close flags → report), the Register as the authoritative record, and the pressed object sampled at every change. The session opened with three author-ruled items carried from register 1760, to be taken one at a time with full ruling requests before implementation.

The three items were resolved in order. First, §34.4 "The rule" in the Löwdin chapter: the author confirmed the chapter is entirely original to this project and directed Claude to write the best wording — the rule, its derivation, attribution, and function in the Löwdin solution — and reframe surrounding references to point to §34.4 as the canonical statement. Claude wrote and implemented a four-part body (what it is, how it was derived, whose it is, its function), added a deferral line to §34.1, and registered ruling 24 (register 1761). Second, F.4.2's "surviving claim" definition, open in Q since register 297: the author chose option D, generalising §D.5.3's move book-wide. Claude encoded the definition in appf.py so F.4.2's census, numerator, and ruled row are press-recomputed at every build; registered ruling 25 (register 1762); and noted that main now carries three numeric register counts that move together. Third, Spectra's 489 untested rows: the author directed that the sealed test instrument from The Method Löwdin project applies (strict interval membership, quotation floor as the only ε, §22.5 admissibility, with option B rejected on four registered grounds). The author provided the spectra_levels_store.zip and then the full restore-point-2_13.tar.gz directly. Claude verified both by sha256 (08a6a78c and 80577094, 708 files), ran the bracket over the 489 rows, and closed 318: 658 of 813 cells pass, 155 fail across 92 rows, zero refused, 68 no-triple. 171 rows remain untested for data reasons — 126 unreconciled (member selection not blind-reproducible from spectra_raw) and 45 belonging to six post-restore-point species. Ruling 26 was registered (register 1763).

During Spectra pressing, Claude discovered that 532 channel rows had printed as literal pipe text in every prior press — found only by sampling the pressed object at the changed rows. The fix was tool-side: build.py received a cont_tables() pass that re-heads headerless pipe-table continuation blocks, with a blank line inserted so pandoc cannot absorb the table into the preceding paragraph. This was registered as entry 1764. The session closed with register at 1,557 entries (165–1764), rulings 24–26 closed, main at 249 pp (stable), Register at 354 pp, Spectra at 21 pp, BUILD-10 bundles assembled and verified by round-trip split, and HANDOFF-11 written leading bundle 2. The author asked for a precise statement of what to request from The Method Löwdin project for the two remaining live items; Claude produced REQUEST-SPECTRA-DATA.md enumerating all 171 rows.

## RULING REQUEST 1 of 3 — §34.4 "The rule": approve, reword, or remove

### The text at issue, in full

The heading `### 34.4 The rule` stood empty from the start of the record until chat 8. Register 1755 recorded it as owed: *"§34.4 'The rule' is a heading with no body between §34.3 and §34.5, and nothing in the register, the Physics Compendium or the main text says what rule it held — a body, or the heading's removal, is the author's."* Chat 8 then wrote a body (register 1756: *"drawn only from §34.1's box and §34.5–34.6"*), and register 1760 holds it as yours: *"whether §34.4's new body says what he meant the rule section to say."* The body as it now stands in the main volume:

> **34.4 The rule**
>
> Stated once, in the form §34.5 to §34.7 use it. For each candidate subshell (n, ℓ) with occupancy q < 2(2ℓ+1),
>
> > **ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**,  **and the incoming electron takes the least ν.**
>
> Its inputs are the candidate's own n, ℓ and q — Pauli's capacity and the count of states below, nothing measured — and one number, *a*, carried from the previous element and reset only at a subshell opening, an aufbau exception or the return from one (§34.6). By §34.3 the rule is a statement on the walk: c is fixed, Z and Nₑ move together, and the rule chooses the valence shell. It does not name n+ℓ. The observed order enters once, through *a*: §34.5 turns "the observed subshell has least ν" into a corridor for *a*, and §34.6 walks *a* through it. Where the order agrees with n+ℓ the rule reproduces n+ℓ; where it does not (§34.1's two inversions) the rule reproduces the order.

### What this is, plainly

Chapter 34 answers Löwdin's challenge. §34.1 shows the formula inside an argument about Madelung's two inversions; §34.5–34.7 then use "the rule" repeatedly (the corridor, the walk, the entry point) without ever having stated it as a standalone object. §34.4 is the one place the rule is supposed to stand alone, stated once, cleanly. The record couldn't write it because no prior text said what that section held — so chat 8 assembled a restatement strictly from what §34.1, §34.3, §34.5 and §34.6 already say. I have verified every claim in it against those sections: the formula matches §34.1's box character-for-character; the three reset triggers match §34.6's list; the walk claim matches §34.3's ladder table. It introduces nothing new — which is exactly why the record cannot approve it: faithfulness to the surrounding text is checkable, but whether it says what *you* meant the section to say is not.

### What your ruling decides downstream

- **Sections:** §34.4 only. Nothing anywhere cites §34.4 (I checked all eight volumes' sources); §34.5–34.7 read unchanged under approval or rewording.
- **Register and counts:** any ruling gets a register entry (following rulings 21–23's pattern) → register moves 1,553 → 1,554, `kinds.py --write` runs, and main's 15 prose + 2 numeric count sentences move with it.
- **Presses:** main and Register both re-press (main for the count sentences and, if reworded, the body; Register for the new entry), each sampled at the change.
- **Tables/figures:** none touched under A or B.

### Options

**A — Approve as written.** The body is verifiably faithful to the record and adds no unverifiable claim. Trade-off: it is deliberately redundant — the same formula prints in §34.1's box one page earlier, and a reader may feel §34.4 repeats rather than crystallises. That redundancy is also its function ("stated once, in the form §34.5–34.7 use it").

**B — Reword.** You supply the wording, or direct changes, and it is set verbatim. Trade-off: one extra segment of work, but the section then says what only you can know it should say — this is the only option that closes the actual open question (authorial intent) rather than the textual one.

**C — Remove the heading** (1755's stated alternative). Trade-off: leaves a numbering gap 34.3 → 34.5, or forces renumbering §34.5–34.10, which touches 6 cross-references (4 in main, 2 in Register — and Register bodies are never edited, so those two would need a correcting entry, not an edit). C is now strictly worse than it was in 1755, because a faithful body exists.

### Recommendation

**A**, unless the body misses your intent on one specific point I'd flag for your eye: the sentence *"By §34.3 the rule is a statement on the walk"* is the body's only interpretive move — it locates the rule on one of §34.3's four ladders. That is consistent with the record but it is a framing choice, not a quotation. If that framing is what you meant, approve; if the rule was meant to be ladder-neutral, reword that one sentence and keep the rest.

---

content.text:
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"
Löwdin asked for the n+ℓ rule. **The rule is not what atoms obey.**

Read from the observed ground configurations of all 108 neutrals, the sequence in
which subshells OPEN is

> 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s **5d 4f** 6p 7s **6d 5f** 7p

**Madelung's rule inverts 5d/4f and 6d/5f.** Lanthanum opens 5d at Z = 57 and 4f
does not appear until cerium; actinium opens 6d at Z = 89 and 5f not until
protactinium. *Seventeen of nineteen openings agree; two do not.*

**So deriving n+ℓ exactly would mean deriving something false at two elements.**
The target is the ORDER, and n+ℓ is a name for it that is 89% accurate.

> **ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**
>
> **The incoming electron occupies the subshell of least ν among those with
> q < 2(2ℓ+1).**

**Both Pauli quantities appear.** The capacity 2(2ℓ+1) governs admissibility AND
sits inside the radicand. *The radicand is the count of states below: complete
lower shells of the same ℓ, plus the fraction of the current one already filled.*

**And the occupancy enters only through Pauli.** With the fraction q/2(2ℓ+1) in the
radicand the scatter in a within a subshell falls from 0.187 to 0.041 at 3p, 0.119
to 0.028 at 4p, 0.088 to 0.018 at 5p, 0.059 to 0.021 at 6p, 0.086 to 0.047 at 5d.
**Raw occupancy makes every one worse.** *The law needs no new coordinate.*

### 34.2 The three bodies, and the pair that has no variable

A Rydberg atom is three bodies — a nucleus, a core of Nₑ−1 electrons, and one
outer electron — and the equation's shape follows from how they are indexed.

**Λ_var** places every variable of the problem on (body, role). **E = 0.**

| body | input | intermediate | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **nucleus** | Z | · | · |
| **core** | Nₑ | ℓ_core, n_out | · |
| **core + rydberg** | · | p, n₀, T | · |
| **nucleus + core** | c | u | · |
| **rydberg** | ℓ | · | δ |
| **nucleus + rydberg** | **—** | **—** | **—** |

> **No variable in the index relates the Rydberg electron to the nucleus

> collapse variable u — is a nucleus–core quantity that the Rydberg electron then
> reads.

**That is the screening statement appearing as a fact about the coordinates**, and
it is a claim about the index and not about the interaction: *the nucleus does
attract the outer electron, and strongly. What the index says is that no
COORDINATE of this problem carries that attraction unmediated.*

**And the channel equation has exactly that shape.** δ = √p · f(u) is a
core–rydberg factor times a nucleus–core factor, **with no third factor because
the index holds no third pair.**

### 34.3 What the ladders can and cannot reach

Because **Z = Nₑ + c − 1**, only two of the three electronic quantities are
independent. **A ladder fixing one varies the other two, and no ladder can vary Z
alone.**

| ladder | fixes | varies | reaches |
|---|---|---|---|
| **isoelectronic** | Nₑ | Z and c | the valence shell |
| **the walk** | c | Z and Nₑ | the valence shell |
| **ionisation** | Z | Nₑ and c | the subvalence shell |
| **isotopic** | **Z, Nₑ and c** | the neutron number | **the nucleus** |

**Three ladders exhaust the electronic space.** *The fourth is orthogonal to all
three, is the only route to the nucleus, and has never been traced.*

Stated once, in the form §34.5 to §34.7 use it. For each candidate subshell (n, ℓ) with occupancy
q < 2(2ℓ+1),

> **ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**,  **and the incoming electron takes the least ν.**

Its inputs are the candidate's own n, ℓ and q — Pauli's capacity and the count of states below,
nothing measured — and one number, *a*, carried from the previous element and reset only at a
subshell opening, an aufbau exception or the return from one (§34.6). By §34.3 the rule is a
statement on the walk: c is fixed, Z and Nₑ move together, and the rule chooses the valence shell.

has least ν" into a corridor for *a*, and §34.6 walks *a* through it. Where the order agrees with n+ℓ
the rule reproduces n+ℓ; where it does not (§34.1's two inversions) the rule reproduces the order.

Requiring the observed subshell to have least ν gives one linear inequality per
rival, and their intersection is an interval:

> **L(Z) < a < U(Z)**,  **L, U = Δn(√p_g + √p_r)/(p_g − p_r)**

**All 106 non-empty. Nineteen distinct surds across the whole table. No
measurement enters — only Pauli's capacity and the node count.**

*For every ns/(n−1)d competition the crossing is (√(n−1) + √(n−4))/3, giving
0.5773503, 1.0000000, 1.2168450, 1.3938270 at n = 4 to 7.*

**`a` is carried between elements and resets eighteen times.** Every reset is a
**subshell opening** (8), an **aufbau exception** (6), or the **return from one**
(4) — Tc after Mo, Tb after Gd, Bk after Cm, Hg after Au. **It never resets
mid-subshell**, which is why each subshell fills at constant `a`.

**And the state is necessary.** With no carried value, 104 of 106 steps admit two
to four self-consistent subshells. *The observed one is always among them and
never uniquely determined. The periodic table is not computable from a single
atom's configuration.*

### 34.7 The entry point

Where `a` sits in its corridor is fixed by the single-state observation — the
ionisation energy — and the position is

> **t(ℓ) → √( ℓ(ℓ+1) / 2 )**

**Measured 1.028 at p across four subshells and 1.785 at d across two: the ratio
is √3 to 0.19%.** *ℓ(ℓ+1) is the centrifugal term, the only place ℓ enters the
radial Schrödinger equation.*

**And it is a limit approached along n**, not a constant: the p row of Λ_t reads
1.120, 1.049, 1.022, 1.002 at n = 3, 4, 5, 6 — **6p sits 0.2% above the
centrifugal value.**

| term | source |
|---|---|
| **n − ℓ − 1** | the node theorem |
| **2(2ℓ+1)** | antisymmetry, twice |
| **ℓ(ℓ+1)** | the centrifugal term, from the angular separation |
| **the energy of a single state** | the observation that fixes what the ordering bounds |
| **the endpoints** | arithmetic on the above |

**No parameter is fitted.**

**Exceptionless on 106 elements**, Z = 3 to 108, including every aufbau anomaly,
**and right where n+ℓ is wrong.**

**f is outside the domain and the law says so.** At any f opening p = n−ℓ−1 = 0,
the floor of the node count — no subshell has fewer nodes than none — **so no
rival lies below and L = −∞.** The quantity t = (a−L)/(U−L) does not exist there.
*The missing test is forbidden by the node count, not by missing data.*

---

### 34.10 How the method delivered it

*This is the part of the chapter the book exists for.*

**The cypher located the split.** Asked of the two halves of `a`, the crossing has
order, algebra and geometry and **no analysis or statistics language**; the descent
has all four. **A quantity that is ordinal, algebraic and geometric but not
analytic is an integer object: it cannot be fitted and needs no fitting.** *Every
fit of the session had been applied to the whole of `a` — which is why the
constants kept absorbing each other. Half the object was a set of surds, and the
parameters were competing to represent them.*

work in the universal column, so **a pooled fit across regions asserts a universal
parameter the closed index says cannot exist.** Replayed against the session's own
work, the protocol blocks the ℓ-spread on six hand-picked species, the amplitude
Gaussian across the whole table, and six occupancy slopes pooled for one scaling —
**and passes the same two objects measured per cell.**

both routed to their chemical property and their class, **and both closed as
withdrawals rather than as answers** — the f corridor is structurally forbidden,
and the 1.029 was arithmetic.

was reported before the selection rule was tested. **Seven of eight rules give
106/106, and random interior points on 200 of 200 seeds.** *The corridor is forced;

## RULING REQUEST 1 of 3 — §34.4 "The rule": approve, reword, or remove

### The text at issue, in full

The heading `### 34.4 The rule` stood empty from the start of the record until chat 8. Register 1755 recorded it as owed: *"§34.4 'The rule' is a heading with no body between §34.3 and §34.5, and nothing in the register, the Physics Compendium or the main text says what rule it held — a body, or the heading's removal, is the author's."* Chat 8 then wrote a body (register 1756: *"drawn only from §34.1's box and §34.5–34.6"*), and register 1760 holds it as yours: *"whether §34.4's new body says what he meant the rule section to say."* The body as it now stands in the main volume:

> **34.4 The rule**
>
> Stated once, in the form §34.5 to §34.7 use it. For each candidate subshell (n, ℓ) with occupancy q < 2(2ℓ+1),
>
> > **ν(n,ℓ,q) = n − a·√( n − ℓ − 1 + q/2(2ℓ+1) )**,  **and the incoming electron takes the least ν.**
>
> Its inputs are the candidate's own n, ℓ and q — Pauli's capacity and the count of states below, nothing measured — and one number, *a*, carried from the previous element and reset only at a subshell opening, an aufbau exception or the return from one (§34.6). By §34.3 the rule is a statement on the walk: c is fixed, Z and Nₑ move together, and the rule chooses the valence shell. It does not name n+ℓ. The observed order enters once, through *a*: §34.5 turns "the observed subshell has least ν" into a corridor for *a*, and §34.6 walks *a* through it. Where the order agrees with n+ℓ the rule reproduces n+ℓ; where it does not (§34.1's two inversions) the rule reproduces the order.

### What this is, plainly

Chapter 34 answers Löwdin's challenge. §34.1 shows the formula inside an argument about Madelung's two inversions; §34.5–34.7 then use "the rule" repeatedly (the corridor, the walk, the entry point) without ever having stated it as a standalone object. §34.4 is the one place the rule is supposed to stand alone, stated once, cleanly. The record couldn't write it because no prior text said what that section held — so chat 8 assembled a restatement strictly from what §34.1, §34.3, §34.5 and §34.6 already say. I have verified every claim in it against those sections: the formula matches §34.1's box character-for-character; the three reset triggers match §34.6's list; the walk claim matches §34.3's ladder table. It introduces nothing new — which is exactly why the record cannot approve it: faithfulness to the surrounding text is checkable, but whether it says what *you* meant the section to say is not.

### What your ruling decides downstream

- **Sections:** §34.4 only. Nothing anywhere cites §34.4 (I checked all eight volumes' sources); §34.5–34.7 read unchanged under approval or rewording.
- **Register and counts:** any ruling gets a register entry (following rulings 21–23's pattern) → register moves 1,553 → 1,554, `kinds.py --write` runs, and main's 15 prose + 2 numeric count sentences move with it.
- **Presses:** main and Register both re-press (main for the count sentences and, if reworded, the body; Register for the new entry), each sampled at the change.
- **Tables/figures:** none touched under A or B.

### Options

**A — Approve as written.** The body is verifiably faithful to the record and adds no unverifiable claim. Trade-off: it is deliberately redundant — the same formula prints in §34.1's box one page earlier, and a reader may feel §34.4 repeats rather than crystallises. That redundancy is also its function ("stated once, in the form §34.5–34.7 use it").

**B — Reword.** You supply the wording, or direct changes, and it is set verbatim. Trade-off: one extra segment of work, but the section then says what only you can know it should say — this is the only option that closes the actual open question (authorial intent) rather than the textual one.

**C — Remove the heading** (1755's stated alternative). Trade-off: leaves a numbering gap 34.3 → 34.5, or forces renumbering §34.5–34.10, which touches 6 cross-references (4 in main, 2 in Register — and Register bodies are never edited, so those two would need a correcting entry, not an edit). C is now strictly worse than it was in 1755, because a faithful body exists.

### Recommendation

**A**, unless the body misses your intent on one specific point I'd flag for your eye: the sentence *"By §34.3 the rule is a statement on the walk"* is the body's only interpretive move — it locates the rule on one of §34.3's four ladders. That is consistent with the record but it is a framing choice, not a quotation. If that framing is what you meant, approve; if the rule was meant to be ladder-neutral, reword that one sentence and keep the rest.

---

## RULING REQUEST 2 of 3 — F.4.2: the definition of a *surviving claim*

### The text at issue, in full

Register 297 (the entry that opened it):

> **THE IDEAL WITHDRAWAL RATIO DERIVED AS 1 : 1 — AT PARITY A CLAIM'S SURVIVAL CARRIES EXACTLY ONE BIT — AND FOUND UNMEASURABLE: THE DENOMINATOR SPANS A FACTOR OF SEVENTY-FIVE DEPENDING ON WHAT A *CLAIM* IS.** **The register cannot count its own denominator.**

F.4.2's measurement section:

> **Measured, the book does not have one answer. It has a bracket.** 190 claim-numbers stand in the register. What stands against them depends entirely on what a surviving claim is, and the book has never said:
>
> | surviving claims taken as | count | ratio | p(survive) | bits |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Appendix D's mathematical elements | 77 | 2.47 : 1 | 0.288 | 0.867 |
> | those plus the Index's terms | 128 | 1.48 : 1 | 0.403 | 0.972 |
> | every claim-bearing number in Appendix F | 6,654 | 0.03 : 1 | 0.972 | 0.183 |
>
> **What would settle it is a definition, not a measurement.** §D.5.3 closed the oldest item in Q by saying what an element is; the same move is available here and has not been made. Until *claim* is defined as *element* was, the withdrawal ratio has no value, only a range… Entered in Q. Register 297.

### What this is, plainly

F.4.2 derives that a register is most informative when withdrawn and surviving claims stand at 1 : 1 — at parity, "this claim survived" is worth exactly one bit. The 190 withdrawn claim-numbers are countable. The survivors are not, because "claim" was never defined, and the three candidate readings differ by a factor of eighty-six. The record cannot settle this because it is a definition, not a computation — the exact move §D.5.3 made for *element* ("a mathematical statement that (i) the book asserts on its own authority; (ii) the book labels; (iii) is taken at the granularity of the result and not of the numbers it yields; (iv) stands at the time of writing"). Nothing in any volume supplies the analogous four clauses for *claim*. `appf.py` line 70 already computes the widest row (n against the fixed 190) at every press and stands ready to compute whatever you define.

### What your ruling decides downstream

- **F.4.2's body**: the bracket paragraph and closing paragraph get their resolution; the table becomes one definition-backed row (with the bracket kept as history) or stays a bracket by ruling.
- **appf.py**: the definition is encoded so F.4.2 is press-recomputed like the rest of Appendix F.
- **The Q item** (open since register 297): closes, or closes-as-ruled-open. It was never entered in E.1.2's table, so no table row moves there unless you want it retro-entered as history.
- **A downstream flag your ruling exposes**: the numerator 190 is a static figure from when F.4.2 was written. Once the denominator has a definition, symmetry invites recounting the numerator by the same standard at this build — I'd propose doing so in the same segment, stated as a dated re-reading.
- **Register/counts/presses**: ruling 25 entered, counts 1,554 → 1,555, main re-pressed and sampled.

### Options

**A — Elements (D.5.3's definition, as it stands).** Survivors = Appendix D's elements: 77, ratio 2.47 : 1. *Trade-off:* the strictest already-printed definition, perfect granularity match with register claim-numbers — but it counts only the mathematics; the book's physics claims vanish from the census, so the ratio overstates withdrawal.

**B — Elements plus the Index's terms (128, 1.48 : 1).** *Trade-off:* the middle reading, closest to parity — but it unions two different granularities (results and terms), which D.5.3's clause (iii) was written to forbid; it would be a bracket midpoint wearing a definition's clothes.

**C — Every claim-bearing number in Appendix F** (6,654 at chat 8's press; press-recomputed). *Trade-off:* fully machine-countable today, zero new work — but it counts occurrences, not claims: one result printed ten times survives ten times. It contradicts the granularity principle the record already ruled for elements, and at 0.03 : 1 it declares survival nearly free of information.

**D — Generalise D.5.3 book-wide: a SURVIVING CLAIM is a statement the book asserts on its own authority, labels (a compendium object, a theorem/element label, or a register-cited claim-number), taken at the granularity of the result, standing at the time of writing.** Operationally: the census is Appendix D's elements plus the standing objects of the compendia — the record's own architecture supplies this (the Register front matter: withdrawn claims live in the register, "the compendia answer"). *Trade-off:* the most principled and the one that closes Q the way D.5.3 closed its item; costs a small counting script over the compendium object labels, and the count is new (I'd estimate order 150–250, landing the ratio near parity — but that is an estimate, not a measurement, until the script runs).

**E — Rule the bracket to be the answer.** Declare *surviving claim* deliberately undefined; F.4.2 prints the bracket as its permanent form and the Q item closes as "ruled unmeasurable." *Trade-off:* honest and cheap, but the register then permanently "cannot count its own denominator" by choice, and the 1 : 1 derivation stays a prediction with no measurement ever to meet it.

It repeats the record's own successful precedent, matches numerator and denominator at the same granularity, makes the row press-recomputable, and closes a Q item that has stood since register 297. If you'd rather not mint a new definition, **A** is the defensible fallback — already printed, already counted — with its mathematics-only scope stated in the row's caption. If you choose D, also tell me whether to recount the 190 numerator by the same standard (I recommend yes, both readings dated).

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## 34. The Löwdin challenge

*In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin set a challenge: derive the n+ℓ filling rule from the
Schrödinger equation. It has stood since. This chapter states the challenge, what
the method delivered, and how the method itself did the work.*

### 34.1 The problem, and the wrong target
===
### 34.10 How the method delivered it

*This is the part of the chapter the book exists for.*

**The cypher located the split.** Asked of the two halves of `a`, the crossing has
order, algebra and geometry and **no analysis or statistics language**; the descent
has all four. **A quantity that is ordinal, algebraic and geometric but not
analytic is an integer object: it cannot be fitted and needs no fitting.** *Every
fit of the session had been applied to the whole of `a` — which is why the
constants kept absorbing each other. Half the object was a set of surds, and the
parameters were competing to represent them.*

**The domain protocol blocked four fits.** Λ_phys closes with no parameter of this
work in the universal column, so **a pooled fit across regions asserts a universal
parameter the closed index says cannot exist.** Replayed against the session's own
work, the protocol blocks the ℓ-spread on six hand-picked species, the amplitude
Gaussian across the whole table, and six occupancy slopes pooled for one scaling —
**and passes the same two objects measured per cell.**

**Λ_chem dissolved two residuals.** The 1.029 factor and the missing f test were
both routed to their chemical property and their class, **and both closed as
withdrawals rather than as answers** — the f corridor is structurally forbidden,
and the 1.029 was arithmetic.

**The falsification withdrew a result.** Eighteen resets landing on exact surds
was reported before the selection rule was tested. **Seven of eight rules give
106/106, and random interior points on 200 of 200 seeds.** *The corridor is forced;
the trajectory was mine.*

**And the one microscope caught the largest thing.** ℓ(ℓ+1) had been recorded four
separate times — as the gate, the collapse switch, the barrier and Seaton's ratio —
before it appeared a fifth and sixth time in the angular factor 1/(2ℓ+1) and the
entry point √(ℓ(ℓ+1)/2). **One object, six appearances, and each had been given a
different discipline's name.**

---

*A Rydberg atom is three bodies: a nucleus, a core of Nₑ−1 electrons, and one
outer electron. The method's contribution is not a solution to the general
three-body problem but a statement about which pairs exist — Chapter 36 takes this up.*

---

## 35. The Löwdin solution

*Chapter 34 stated the law that names the order — the corridor, the walk, and the
entry point, read from the table's own coordinates with one observation per
===LOWDIN===
4:### A Formal Response to the 1969 Löwdin Challenge
13:In 1969 Per-Olov Löwdin challenged theoretical physics to derive the ordering rules of the periodic table — the Madelung (n+ℓ) filling rule, the period-length sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and the Aufbau principle itself — directly from the many-electron Schrödinger equation, with no empirical parameters of any kind. This paper presents a solution. A sequential, parameter-free construction is defined in which the electron that differentiates element Z from element Z−1 is placed in the self-consistent field of the atom that preceded it, and the orbital channel it occupies is determined by that field alone. Executed across the entire table with the inverse fine-structure constant c = 137.035999 as the only number supplied, the construction reproduces the observed filling order at all 107 elements for which ground configurations are known (Z = 2–108), locates the three genuine exceptions to the secondary rule exactly where nature has them and derives them from the physics of orbital collapse, proves that no g block exists anywhere below Z = 121, and shows that the observed table is irreducibly relativistic: with the speed of light taken to infinity, the same construction misplaces eleven elements, silver and mercury among them. Second-order correlation corrections are computed at every element where the mean-field competition is close, and in every case they widen, rather than overturn, the derived order. Beyond the last measured element the same construction issues twelve falsifiable predictions (Z = 109–120) that reproduce the relativistic Dirac–Fock shell sequence. {"returncode":0,"stdout":"# Register front matter, "What the entries are": counts of entries whose HEADLINE matches each pattern
# (case-insensitive; a body tag "(a finding.)" etc. overrides). Kinds overlap; not a partition. Register 1756.
import re,collections,sys
R=open(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv)>1 else 'The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md',encoding='utf-8').read()
i=R.find('\n### 165\n'); body=R[i:]
ents=re.split(r'\n### ([\d, a-z]+)\n',body)
ids,bodies=ents[1::2],ents[2::2]
PAT={
 'a correction':   r'CORRECT|WRONG|STALE|PUT RIGHT|AMEND|FIX|MISLOCAT|REPAIR|ERROR|OVERTAKEN|MISTAK|MISREAD|MISCOUNT',
 'a measurement':  r'\d',
 'prior art':      r'PRIOR ART|PUBLISHED|ALREADY (KNOWN|IN|DONE)|\b(1[5-9]\d\d|20[0-2]\d)\b|[A-Z][a-z]+ \(\d{4}\)',
 'a new protocol': r'PROTOCOL|\bRULE\b|RULED|RULING|MUST\b|NEVER AGAIN|PROCEDURE',
 'a withdrawal':   r'WITHDR|RETRACT|REMOVED|DROPPED|ABANDON|DISCARD',
 'a fault of mine':r'FAULT OF MINE|MY FAULT|MY ERROR|THE ASSISTANT|I (MIS|FAIL|WROTE|CARRIED)|MEA CULPA',
 'an open question':r'OPEN QUESTION|\bOPEN\b|UNSETTLED|CANNOT (CURRENTLY|YET)|UNKNOWN|UNRESOLVED|NOT (YET )?(SETTLED|KNOWN)',
}
TAG=r'\(\s*(a finding|a correction|a measurement|prior art|a new protocol|a withdrawal|a fault of mine|an open question)\.?\s*\)\*?\s*$'
cnt=collections.Counter()
for i,b in zip(ids,bodies):
    b=b.strip(); head=re.match(r'\*\*(.*?)\*\*',b,re.S); head=head.group(1) if head else b[:200]
    kinds={k for k,p in PAT.items() if re.search(p,head,re.I)}
    t=re.findall(TAG,b)
    if t: kinds={t[-1]}
    if ',' in i: kinds|={'a correction','a fault of mine'}   # grouped early fault entries, by mechanism
    if not (kinds & {'a correction','a withdrawal','a fault of mine','an open question'}): kinds.add('a finding')
    for k in kinds: cnt[k]+=1
print(len(ids),dict(cnt))
if '--write' in sys.argv:   # rewrite the Build 9 column and the heading count in the Register front matter
    R2=R
    for k,n in cnt.items():
        R2,c=re.subn(r'(\| \*\*'+re.escape(k)+r'\*\* \| )[\d,]+( \| )',lambda m:m.group(1)+f'{n:,}'+m.group(2),R2,count=1); assert c==1,k
    R2,c=re.subn(r'over the [\d,]+ entry headings',f'over the {len(ids):,} entry headings',R2); assert c==1
    open(sys.argv[1],'w',encoding='utf-8').write(R2); print('written')
","stderr":""}

content.text:
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"11141:34.4 The rule
===
What it is. An occupation law: at each step of the periodic table it selects the subshell the differentiating
electron enters — the ORDER of §34.1, named exactly. Its inputs are the candidate’s own n, ℓ and q — the
node count and Pauli’s capacity, nothing measured — and one number, a, carried from the previous element
and reset only at a subshell opening, an aufbau exception or the return from one (§34.6). By §34.3 it is a
statement on the walk: c is fixed, Z and Nₑ move together, and the rule chooses the valence shell.

 How it was derived. Read from the observed ground configurations of the 108 neutrals, not from a fit;
§34.10 gives the session that did it. The radicand is the count of states below — the node theorem supplies n −
ℓ − 1 and antisymmetry the capacity 2(2ℓ+1), twice — and the observed order enters once, through a: §34.5
turns “the observed subshell has least ν” into a corridor, and §34.6 walks a through it. No parameter is
fitted; the provenance of every term is §34.8’s table.
Whose it is. The rule it replaces is not this work’s: n+ℓ belongs to Madelung (1936), to Janet (1929) before
him, and to Klechkovskii — and the demand for its derivation is Löwdin’s (1969). The ν rule is this record’s
own, first stated in this work.
Its function in the Löwdin solution. It re-poses the target. Deriving n+ℓ exactly would derive something
false at two elements (§34.1); ν names the observed order at all of them, so what Chapter 35 and the paper
derive is the order ν names, not the name that is 89% accurate. Where the order agrees with n+ℓ the rule
reproduces n+ℓ; where it does not — §34.1’s two inversions — the rule reproduces the order.
","stderr":""}

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"### 297

**THE IDEAL WITHDRAWAL RATIO DERIVED AS 1 : 1 — AT PARITY A CLAIM'S SURVIVAL CARRIES EXACTLY ONE BIT — AND FOUND UNMEASURABLE: THE DENOMINATOR SPANS A FACTOR OF SEVENTY-FIVE DEPENDING ON WHAT A *CLAIM* IS.** **The register cannot count its own denominator.**

### 298
===F42===
### F.4.2 The ideal withdrawal ratio is 1 : 1
 §F.4.1 measures the withdrawal ratio in words and leaves the number uninterpreted. Words are a proxy.
 The quantity is a ratio of **claims**, and on that basis the ideal has a derivation rather than a
 preference.

    **A claim's survival carries information, and 1 : 1 is where it carries the most.** If
    withdrawals and survivors stand in ratio r, the chance a given claim survives is 1/(1 + r), and
    the news that it did carries −p log₂p − (1−p)log₂(1−p) bits. That is maximal at p = ½, which is
    r = 1. **Below 1 : 1 survival is cheap news** — almost everything survives, so surviving says
    little. **Above it, withdrawal is cheap** — the record is mostly failure and the process is
    spending more than it keeps. At parity, the fact that a claim stands is worth exactly one bit,
    and that is the most a register can ever tell a reader about any single claim in it.

 **Measured, the book does not have one answer. It has a bracket.** 190 claim-numbers stand in the
 register. What stands against them depends entirely on what a surviving claim is, and the book has
 never said:

  surviving claims taken as                     count      ratio        p(survive)   bits
  Appendix D's mathematical elements               77     2.47 : 1          0.288    0.867
  those plus the Index's terms                    128     1.48 : 1          0.403    0.972
  every claim-bearing number in Appendix F      6,654     0.03 : 1          0.972    0.183

 **The three readings span a factor of eighty-six, and 1 : 1 lies inside them.** That is a bracket
 in this book's own sense: the quantity is bounded by measured neighbours and undetermined between
 them, so the prediction is **consistent with the evidence and not established by it** — which is
 precisely what §22 says a bracket means and precisely the standing §25.6 has.

 **What would settle it is a definition, not a measurement.** §D.5.3 closed the oldest item in Q by
 saying what an element is; the same move is available here and has not been made. Until *claim* is
 defined as *element* was, the withdrawal ratio has no value, only a range — and the register, which
 exists to make the book's failures countable, cannot count its own denominator. Entered in Q.
 Register 297.

### F.4.3 Time, which this book already has and does not read

===F41===
### F.4.1 Two ratios the book had never measured about itself
 Appendix F indexes the numbers this book prints and had not indexed the two that describe its own
 shape. They are named here because a quantity without a name cannot be tracked, and both are
 measurements the method demands of anything else it examines.

    **The withdrawal ratio.** Words of register against words of argument — Chapter 28 against every other chapter of the book. **0.445 when first measured (register 296), 0.249 after the register was compressed
    (register 363), and a press readout since register 374.** Those readings were taken while the entries lived inside Chapter 28. The Register is now its own volume (register 1725), so the ratio has two readings and the book prints both, dated: **Chapter 28 against every other chapter, 5,704 : 108,630 = 0.053**, which measures only the chapter that discusses the withdrawals; and **the Register volume against the main volume, 197,651 : 114,334 = 1.73**, which is the like-for-like successor of 0.445 and 0.249 (both recomputed 2026-08-24 from the files). At the second reading the record is larger than the argument, and that is stated rather than hidden in a chapter count.

    **The method ratio.** Words of Part I — the twenty principles, the twenty-four protocols,
    the twenty-five prime audits — against the whole book but for itself. **12,663 : 101,671 = 0.125** (2026-08-24; 11,811 : 75,459 = 0.157 when first measured). Against the
    six appendices alone it is 0.800: the machinery is now very nearly the size of all the
    mathematics it audits.

 **What each is for.** §32.1.1's fourth referee flag says the register is longer than the results and
 the book has no answer to the fair version of the question. The withdrawal ratio is that question
 made numeric: at 0.249 the register was a quarter of the argument and at 1.73 it is larger than the argument, and the flag asked not whether that is
 large but **whether it is falling**. It is not tracked over time within the record, because entries carry
 no date; the three readings above are dated by the build that took them, and they are not like for like; §32.1.2's split of thirty-four defects to eight self-inflicted is one session's measurement
 and there is no second point. **A ratio with one observation is a number, not a trend**, and that is
 the honest state of referee flag 4.

 The method ratio has no referee behind it and may matter more. Part I has grown faster in these

content.text:
Fetch for Item 2 complete. One detail verified before presenting: the F.4.2 item never reached E.1.2's table — it lives only in F.4.2's prose and register 297.

---

## RULING REQUEST 2 of 3 — F.4.2: the definition of a *surviving claim*

### The text at issue, in full

Register 297 (the entry that opened it):

> **THE IDEAL WITHDRAWAL RATIO DERIVED AS 1 : 1 — AT PARITY A CLAIM'S SURVIVAL CARRIES EXACTLY ONE BIT — AND FOUND UNMEASURABLE: THE DENOMINATOR SPANS A FACTOR OF SEVENTY-FIVE DEPENDING ON WHAT A *CLAIM* IS.** **The register cannot count its own denominator.**

F.4.2's measurement section:

> **Measured, the book does not have one answer. It has a bracket.** 190 claim-numbers stand in the register. What stands against them depends entirely on what a surviving claim is, and the book has never said:
>
> | surviving claims taken as | count | ratio | p(survive) | bits |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Appendix D's mathematical elements | 77 | 2.47 : 1 | 0.288 | 0.867 |
> | those plus the Index's terms | 128 | 1.48 : 1 | 0.403 | 0.972 |
> | every claim-bearing number in Appendix F | 6,654 | 0.03 : 1 | 0.972 | 0.183 |
>
> **What would settle it is a definition, not a measurement.** §D.5.3 closed the oldest item in Q by saying what an element is; the same move is available here and has not been made. Until *claim* is defined as *element* was, the withdrawal ratio has no value, only a range… Entered in Q. Register 297.

### What this is, plainly

F.4.2 derives that a register is most informative when withdrawn and surviving claims stand at 1 : 1 — at parity, "this claim survived" is worth exactly one bit. The 190 withdrawn claim-numbers are countable. The survivors are not, because "claim" was never defined, and the three candidate readings differ by a factor of eighty-six. The record cannot settle this because it is a definition, not a computation — the exact move §D.5.3 made for *element* ("a mathematical statement that (i) the book asserts on its own authority; (ii) the book labels; (iii) is taken at the granularity of the result and not of the numbers it yields; (iv) stands at the time of writing"). Nothing in any volume supplies the analogous four clauses for *claim*. `appf.py` line 70 already computes the widest row (n against the fixed 190) at every press and stands ready to compute whatever you define.

### What your ruling decides downstream

- **F.4.2's body**: the bracket paragraph and closing paragraph get their resolution; the table becomes one definition-backed row (with the bracket kept as history) or stays a bracket by ruling.
- **appf.py**: the definition is encoded so F.4.2 is press-recomputed like the rest of Appendix F.
- **The Q item** (open since register 297): closes, or closes-as-ruled-open. It was never entered in E.1.2's table, so no table row moves there unless you want it retro-entered as history.
- **A downstream flag your ruling exposes**: the numerator 190 is a static figure from when F.4.2 was written. Once the denominator has a definition, symmetry invites recounting the numerator by the same standard at this build — I'd propose doing so in the same segment, stated as a dated re-reading.
- **Register/counts/presses**: ruling 25 entered, counts 1,554 → 1,555, main re-pressed and sampled.

### Options

**A — Elements (D.5.3's definition, as it stands).** Survivors = Appendix D's elements: 77, ratio 2.47 : 1. *Trade-off:* the strictest already-printed definition, perfect granularity match with register claim-numbers — but it counts only the mathematics; the book's physics claims vanish from the census, so the ratio overstates withdrawal.

### What this is, plainly

Each channel row lists a series of measured levels. For every interior member, the two neighbours each imply a quantum defect; those two defects predict a range for the middle member's energy; the bracket asks whether the measured energy falls inside. A tolerance is needed because at strict betweenness the test is known to fail heavily on real data (Chapter 24's strict run: 69.2%, with failures mixing genuine perturbations and mere measurement noise). The builder never stated the tolerance, so 489 of 596 rows honestly say `untested`. The record cannot settle it: a tolerance is a judgement about what counts as agreement, not a computation.

**And there is a second blocker the record forced me to verify before asking you:** the test consumes per-level energies, and those exist in none of the artefacts in reach. The bundles carry only the summary table (δ, σ, ranges); COORDINATES-2_13.csv in Drive carries one δ per cell, no levels; the capture files the register names (`CHANNELS-NEW.tsv`, `MEASUREMENTS.tsv`, `LEVELS-*.tsv`) are in no bundle and not in Drive — the register itself records that store as unregenerable ("the chain survives only as data; neither step's code is in the bank"). **What a surviving claim is — defined at last, the move §D.5.3 made for *element* (ruling 25,
 register 1762).** The bracket below stood from register 297 to register 1761 because the book had
 never said what a claim is. It says now.

    A SURVIVING CLAIM is a statement that (i) the book asserts on its own authority rather than
    importing; (ii) the book labels — an element of Appendix D, or a labelled object of a
    compendium; (iii) is taken at the granularity of the result and not of the numbers it
    yields; and (iv) stands at the time of writing, a statement withdrawn belonging to the
    register and not to the census.

 **The census, on one printed rule, recomputed at press by `appf.py`.** Appendix D's elements, 77;
 the Mathematical Compendium's labelled objects, 265; the Physics Compendium's labelled parameter
 objects, 27 — **369 in all.** The Index of Indices and the Spectra Compendium enter at zero: they
 are index volumes whose content is cells and coordinates, which clause (iii) excludes, and the
 rule says so rather than guessing. The label spaces are disjoint by namespace; where one result
 bears a label in two rosters it counts once per roster, a boundary the rule states rather than
 hides.

 **And the withdrawn side is re-read by the same standard, both readings dated.** 190 claim-numbers
 stood in the register when this section was written (register 297); the rule behind that figure
 was never printed, and it is kept as the reading it was. At this build the count is one withdrawn
 claim per register entry — the book's own sentence, printed fifteen times, that the register's
 claims were made and were wrong — which is the register's entry count, 1,555 at this build,
 recomputed at press from the Register file.

  the ruled reading (2026-08-24)             withdrawn   surviving      ratio   p(survive)   bits
  by the definition above                        1,555         369   4.21 : 1        0.192    0.705

 **The verdict the definition delivers.** The record stands above parity: survival carries 0.705
 bits against the one-bit maximum, and the derivation above already names this side — withdrawal
 is cheap, the record is mostly failure, and the process is spending more than it keeps. That is
 now a measured property of the book, not a range. The bracket is kept as the first reading, dated
 to register 1761:

  surviving claims taken as (first readings)    count      ratio        p(survive)   bits
  Appendix D's mathematical elements               77     2.47 : 1          0.288    0.867
  those plus the Index's terms                    128     1.48 : 1          0.403    0.972
  every claim-bearing number in Appendix F      6,654     0.03 : 1          0.972    0.183

 **The three first readings spanned a factor of eighty-six, and 1 : 1 lay inside them** — a bracket
 in this book's own sense, the quantity bounded by measured neighbours and undetermined between
 them, which is what §22 says a bracket means. The definition collapses it: the second row was two
 granularities in union, the third counted occurrences and not results, and clause (iii) rules on
 both.

 **The definition settled what measurement could not.** §D.5.3 closed the oldest item in Q by
 saying what an element is; the same move is now made here. The item entered in Q at register 297
 — the register, which exists to make the book's failures countable, could not count its own
 denominator — closes at register 1762, ruling 25: it can now, and the number is above.

import math,os
# F.4.2 (ruling 25, register 1762): surviving = D's elements (77, D.5.3/D.5.10's printed count)

# withdrawn = one claim per Register entry (the book's own sentence), the entry heading count.
DELEM=77; B=os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv)>1 else '.'))
MC=os.path.join(B,'The_Method_1_6___Mathematical_Compendium-2.md'); PC=os.path.join(B,'The_Method_1_6___The_Physics_Compendium-2.md'); RG=os.path.join(B,'The_Method_1_6___The_Register-2.md')
if all(os.path.exists(x) for x in (MC,PC,RG)):
    mth=sum(1 for l in open(MC,encoding='utf-8') if l.startswith('### `'))
    phy=sum(1 for l in open(PC,encoding='utf-8') if l.startswith('### '))
    Rt=open(RG,encoding='utf-8').read(); wd=len(re.split(r'\n### ([\d, a-z]+)\n',Rt[Rt.find('\n### 165\n'):])[1::2])
    sv=DELEM+mth+phy; pp=sv/(sv+wd); bits=-(pp*math.log2(pp)+(1-pp)*math.log2(1-pp))
    print(f'F.4.2 ruled row: withdrawn {wd:,}  surviving {sv:,} (77+{mth}+{phy})  {wd/sv:.2f} : 1  p {pp:.3f}  bits {bits:.3f}')
else:

Two channels can both have p = 0 — no core orbitals of their own ℓ — and differ by a factor of ten. Ti IV's nd is **0.6202**; Sr II's nf is **0.0618**.

What separates them is **orbital collapse**, and its threshold is a Janet block boundary exactly:

| orbital | n+ℓ | block opens at | element | collapse threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **3d** | 5 | **Z = 21** | Sc | **21** |
| **4f** | 7 | **Z = 57** | La | **57** |
| **5f** | 8 | **Z = 89** | Ac | **89** |

Across 116 cells with p = 0 at ℓ = 2 or 3: **collapsed median 0.637, uncollapsed 0.036**, U-test p = 9.8×10⁻⁴. The transition is rapid rather than sharp — the largest defects are the atoms *approaching* a boundary: Ca I nd = 0.908 at Z = 20 against a threshold of 21, and Ba II nf = 0.756 at 56 against 57.

**The collapse coordinate is read from the periodic table, not fitted**, and it is why a defect at ℓ = 2 can be large in one element and negligible in its neighbour.

![The channel map](figures-compendia/fig-channel-map.png)

*Every cell valued. The upper panel is δ itself, charge collapsed to its largest; the lower is which mechanism sets it, with the three Janet boundaries marked.*

### A channel is a curve

        δ(n) = δ₀ + δ₂/(n − δ₀)²

**δ₀ is the limit value the index carries; δ₂ is the curvature.** Fitted on 274 channels, the second term removes **48%** of what a constant defect leaves as scatter.

**And the sign of δ₂ names the regime**: positive for core penetration, negative for core polarisation. By orbital: **s 76% positive, p 74%, d 37%, f 6%, g 7%.** *The sign rule is NIST's own, stated in the reference the levels come from. What the compendium adds is the measurement across 274 channels and the finding that |δ₂| predicts a channel's scatter at R² = 0.761.*

![The index](figures-compendia/fig-index-final.png)

**The bracket — T(n) between T(n−1) and T(n+1) — is the book's one ternary object (§21.5.1), and Λ₃ is the ternary object of celestial mechanics.** The two share the deficit: both need strong 3-consistency and both get level 2 from ℛ. In spectra the deficit is paid per channel by the envelope cells of §12.11.3; in three bodies it is paid once, by the stratum boundaries. No channel entry changes. *The same shortfall, on a classical object, is Λ₃ (Index of Indices V; register 1716, 1724).*

1711:**AND THE FIVE READ AS BINARY, WITH TWO EXACT COMPLEMENTS.** *Writing 1 for a coordinate at its maximum and 0 at its minimum:* **corner 1 and corner 2 differ on 3 bits of 3; corner 3 and the unit cell differ on 3 of 3; corner 4 is fully specified at 11001100** *and is the static transition.* **Every one of the eight coordinates receives both a 0 and a 1 across the five, with no column one-sided.** *Measured at one cap setting; whether the pairing survives other caps is untested, so this describes Λ₈ and is not yet a law.*
2379:**`channels.py` WROTE THE BRACKET COLUMN AS `{interior}/{interior}` — PASSING BY CONSTRUCTION, NEVER COMPUTED.** *The bracketing method of Part II reads a cell against its measured neighbours and asks whether the true value falls inside; running it needs those neighbours and a tolerance, and `channels.py` supplies neither.* **285 of 413 channels carried a column that reads like a test result and was a constant.** *It now reads `untested`.* **This is register 695's fault in a new place: not a fabricated measurement, but a fabricated VERIFICATION.**

6621: **Al I *n*f is the first channel to reach its own ceiling.** Predicted 50.7; the four failing cells are *n* = 48, 51, 53, 54 — **per cell, not a range cutoff**, since 49, 50 and 52 pass. The bracket is unaffected in all 94: containment needs only monotonicity, which rounding preserves.
6626: **Two collections, and only one of them is bracket-tested.**
6628: **The bracket has now been run, and it passes 546 of 789 interior cells — 69.2%.** *The test takes the defect each neighbour implies, forms the range they span, and asks whether the middle member's measured energy falls inside. It fails on 243 cells across 62 channels.*
6630:**On the same 789 cells the TRIVIAL bracket — E(n−1) ≤ E(n) ≤ E(n+1) — passes 789 of 789.** *A Rydberg series rises monotonically toward its limit by construction, so that form cannot fail. An earlier version of this chapter read "the bracket holds in every one", and 100% is what the trivial form produces; the implementation behind Appendix B is not in hand, so this is a signature rather than a proof.* **Register 797.**
6634: *An earlier version of this chapter read "1,442 interior cells across 35 atomic systems, the bracket holds in every one." That figure matches neither Appendix B's totals line (1,105) nor its table (869) nor the present tested count (930), and register 673 already recorded that the totals line counts twenty rows the table does not list. **Four numbers for one collection is a disclosure, not a reconciliation** — reconciling needs the twenty rows, which are owed. Register 783.*
6731: H I gives 5 cells with a **median error of 0.006 cm⁻¹** — two orders of magnitude better than anything else here. That figure is not a triumph of the bracket. **It is an identity.**
6746: Cells within a channel share neighbours, so successive brackets are correlated. The honest figure is **1,442 cells across approximately 190 channels.**
6748: **The largest single blocks are the most strongly correlated.** He I's nine channels contribute 189 cells; Ne I's sixteen contribute 131. A reader who discounts within-channel correlation entirely — counting **one effective test per channel** — gets **190 rather than 1,442**, and the bracket holds in all 190.
6755: The ASD marks series-formula values in brackets. Tested against observed values in Al I, derived levels
===

 **The 0.006 cm⁻¹ is therefore a floor on interpretation.** No result in this part can be read as better than the data it rests on, and hydrogen is where that becomes visible because there is nothing else in the way.

### 24.8 On independence, and the most conservative reading
 1,442 cells are not 1,442 independent tests.

 Cells within a channel share neighbours, so successive brackets are correlated. The honest figure is **1,442 cells across approximately 190 channels.**

 **The largest single blocks are the most strongly correlated.** He I's nine channels contribute 189 cells; Ne I's sixteen contribute 131. A reader who discounts within-channel correlation entirely — counting **one effective test per channel** — gets **190 rather than 1,442**, and the bracket holds in all 190.

    That is the most conservative reading available, and it is the one this book would defend.

 **The claim is not that 1,442 independent things were verified.** It is that 190 channels were examined, each exhaustively, and none produced a failure.

### 24.9 A caveat the collection forced
 The ASD marks series-formula values in brackets. Tested against observed values in Al I, derived levels
 bracket exactly as observed ones do — and slightly better.

 **And the caveat is sharper than it was written, on two counts, both established against the ASD
 itself rather than argued.**

| `source` | 32 distinct | the compilation, species and statistic the value was taken from, or the rule that computed it |
| `B` | 0 … 7 | the Pauli bound on δ, read from the ground state; nonzero on 36,917 cells |
| `witness` | witnessed · unwitnessed | 358 · 104,474 — reality consulted, or not |

Every count on these pages is read from the file; none is transcribed.*

supply: at every element, a depth for every frontier channel, computed from the
many-electron field with one constant and no measurement. The two supplies meet
at the same atoms from opposite directions, and where one is silent the other
speaks.*

every later scrutiny is measured against.

content.text:
Fetch for Item 3 complete — including the decisive negative result: **the level store does not exist in any reachable artefact** (container, both bundles, Drive — only COORDINATES-2_13.csv is there, and it holds one δ per cell, no per-n level energies). The ruling request must therefore cover both the tolerance and the data path.

---

## RULING REQUEST 3 of 3 — Spectra's 489 `untested` rows: the tolerance, and the data to run it on

### The text at issue, in full

The count line beneath the channel table (Spectra Compendium, Part II):

> The bracket has been run on 107 rows and holds **844 of 844**; the remaining 489 rows carry `untested`, because the bracketing method needs measured neighbours and a tolerance that the builder does not supply (*What the interface still does not state*, above).

The test's definition, from Chapter 24:

> **The bracket has now been run, and it passes 546 of 789 interior cells — 69.2%.** *The test takes the defect each neighbour implies, forms the range they span, and asks whether the middle member's measured energy falls inside.*

And the history that made `untested` the honest grade — the register records that `channels.py` once wrote the bracket column as `{interior}/{interior}`, *"passing by construction, never computed... running it needs those neighbours and a tolerance, and channels.py supplies neither"* — a fabricated verification, corrected to `untested`.

### What this is, plainly

Each channel row lists a series of measured levels. For every interior member, the two neighbours each imply a quantum defect; those two defects predict a range for the middle member's energy; the bracket asks whether the measured energy falls inside. A tolerance is needed because at strict betweenness the test is known to fail heavily on real data (Chapter 24's strict run: 69.2%, with failures mixing genuine perturbations and mere measurement noise). The builder never stated the tolerance, so 489 of 596 rows honestly say `untested`. The record cannot settle it: a tolerance is a judgement about what counts as agreement, not a computation.

**And there is a second blocker the record forced me to verify before asking you:** the test consumes per-level energies, and those exist in none of the artefacts in reach. The bundles carry only the summary table (δ, σ, ranges); COORDINATES-2_13.csv in Drive carries one δ per cell, no levels; the capture files the register names (`CHANNELS-NEW.tsv`, `MEASUREMENTS.tsv`, `LEVELS-*.tsv`) are in no bundle and not in Drive — the register itself records that store as unregenerable ("the chain survives only as data; neither step's code is in the bank"). So your tolerance alone unlocks the *definition*; the *run* also needs data.

### What your ruling decides downstream

The bracket column of up to 489 rows; the count-line sentence; the compendium's tolerance statement (closing "the builder does not supply"); register entry (ruling 26), counts 1,555 → 1,556 and the three main-volume numeric counts with them; Spectra re-pressed and sampled; main re-pressed for the count sentences.

### Options — the tolerance

**A — τ = 0, strict betweenness.** The pure ternary object. *Trade-off:* known to fail ~31% of cells on clean data; a `fail` would not distinguish a perturbation from last-digit noise, so the column would overstate defects.

**B — τ = 2·σ(δ) per channel, in defect units** (the table's own σ(δ) column widens each row's range). *Trade-off:* computable from the record's own numbers, scales with each channel's scatter (σ spans 0.0008 to 0.08 across rows — one absolute number can't serve both); at k = 2 a true perturbation still fails while noise passes. k = 1 would flag roughly a third of clean cells; k = 3 is nearly blind.

**C — one absolute tolerance on δ (e.g., 0.005).** *Trade-off:* simple and uniform, but too loose for the tightest channels and too tight for the noisiest — it re-imports the pooling fault the record has withdrawn twice elsewhere.

**D — tolerance from source precision (NIST level uncertainties propagated).** *Trade-off:* the most physical, but the uncertainties live in the absent level store; unrunnable today.

### Options — the data path

**1 — You restore the level store** (`captures/` / `CHANNELS-NEW.tsv` / `MEASUREMENTS.tsv` from a restore point or bank you hold). I have reviewed the container, both bundles and Drive first, per protocol — the request is now legitimate. *Cleanest: the run uses the exact levels the table was built from.*

**2 — I refetch levels from NIST ASD by web** for the 489 rows' species. *Trade-off:* the register documents the working URL form, but this rebuilds a capture pipeline whose rules (parent-term walls, J-resolution, excluding NIST's square-bracket interpolated values) are scattered across many entries — large, error-prone, and likely to push this chat past handoff before the presses.

**3 — Close definitionally now, run later:** print the ruled tolerance in the compendium (the interface then *states* it — that defect closes), keep `untested` as the honest grade with the note rewritten to say the only missing ingredient is the level store, and the run happens the day the store returns. *Trade-off:* the 489 stay untested, but honestly and with the blocker halved.

### Recommendation

**B (k = 2) for the tolerance**, because it is the only option both principled and computable from the record's own columns, and **1 for the data if you hold the store — otherwise 3**. I recommend against 2 in this chat: the presses and BUILD-10 bundles must still fit before handoff, and a 489-row refetch would not.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# RULING — Tolerance for the 489-row bracket run

Issued by M (The Method Löwdin project), 2026-08-24, accompanying
`spectra_levels_store.zip` (sha256 08a6a78c…, cut from restore-point-2_13,
bank sha 80577094…, 708 files).

## The ruling

1. **Test.** The bracket test runs at STRICT INTERVAL MEMBERSHIP, exactly as
   the sealed instrument defines it (`bracket.py`, register 796):
   E(n) ∈ [E_lo, E_hi], where the interval is the energy span implied by the
   two neighbours' defects. No statistical tolerance. No k. No σ band.
   This is the condition the run itself stated — "the same test as the 107" —
   and the sealed test carries no tolerance to reproduce.

2. **Boundary guard (the only ε permitted).** Comparisons at the interval
   edges are guarded by the QUOTATION FLOOR: half a unit in the last quoted
   decimal place of the measured level. This is data quantization read off the
   source, not a fitted parameter, and it satisfies the standing floor rule
   (F104.1/F104.2: value-exact comparisons must state and exceed the
   floating-point floor).

3. **Admissibility replaces tolerance.** A cell where the measurement cannot
   distinguish pass from fail is REFUSED, not passed with slack:
   r = 2·Z²R/(ν³σ) ≥ 5 (Method §22.5). Refusals are counted and reported as
   their own column, separate from pass/fail.

4. **Option B (2·σ(δ) per channel, k = 2) is REJECTED**, on four registered
   grounds:
   a. It is a different test than the sealed 930-cell run — violating the
      run's own stated requirement.
   b. It grafts the inferential σ (Rule 4) onto the deductive bracket,
      collapsing Rule 3's separation; a deduction becomes an estimate
      (Method §22.2, §23.3: "V contains no σ").
   c. A tolerance-widened bracket is the registered fault species of a check
      that admits inputs incapable of failing it (registers 777, 782, 784).
   d. The σ it would be built from is measured untrustworthy where it would
      be used: quoted-decimal error estimates drive an 89% result to 55%
      with non-overlapping intervals (register 822); 44 of 49 species carry
      no uncertainty column (register 807); and per-channel σ(δ) computed
      from the data under test is register 781's circularity.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""bracket.py -- run the bracketing test on every channel, for real.

Register 796. `channels.py` wrote the bracket column as {interior}/{interior} —
passing by construction, never computed (register 782). This computes it.

THE TEST. For three consecutive members of a Rydberg series at n-1, n, n+1, the
outer two are used to predict the middle one, and the prediction is a BRACKET, not
a point. The true value either falls inside or it does not.

    from the limit and each neighbour, the quantum defect it implies:
        d(m) = m - Z sqrt(R / (limit - E(m)))
    the two neighbours give d(n-1) and d(n+1); the bracket for the middle is the
    energy range spanned by those two defects:
        E_lo = limit - Z^2 R / (n - min(d(n-1), d(n+1)))^2
        E_hi = limit - Z^2 R / (n - max(d(n-1), d(n+1)))^2
    and the test is whether the MEASURED E(n) lies in [E_lo, E_hi].

WHY THIS CAN FAIL. If the defect were exactly constant the bracket would collapse
to a point and nothing would pass. If the defect varied wildly the bracket would be
wide and everything would pass. It fails when the defect is NOT monotone across the
three — when a perturber sits between them, or when P.lens's amplification makes the
neighbours disagree in the wrong direction. On an unperturbed converging series the
middle defect lies between its neighbours' and the test passes; on a perturbed one it
does not.

The bracket is only defined for INTERIOR members — those with a measured neighbour
on each side. That is what "interior cells" has always counted.
"""
import re, math, glob, os, sys
from collections import defaultdict
from zeno import State, step

R = 109737.31568
LM = {"s":0,"p":1,"d":2,"f":3,"g":4,"h":5,"i":6,"k":7}

def load_limits():
    """Read LIM straight out of channels.py by executing only its assignment.

    Parsing it with a regex assumed the block ends with a newline and a brace; it
    closes inline, so the match failed silently and returned None. Evaluating the
    real object cannot drift from the source (register 796).
    """
    src = open("channels.py", encoding="utf-8").read()
    i = src.index("LIM = {")
    depth, j = 0, i + len("LIM = ")
    while True:
        if src[j] == "{": depth += 1
        elif src[j] == "}":
            depth -= 1
            if depth == 0: break
        j += 1
    return eval(src[i+len("LIM = "):j+1])

def run():
    LIM = load_limits()
    res = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0, []])      # key -> [passed, tested, failures]
    for f in sorted(glob.glob("spectra_raw/*.tsv")):
        nm = os.path.basename(f)[:-4]
        if nm not in LIM: continue
        lim, Z = LIM[nm]
        ser = defaultdict(list)
        for line in open(f, encoding="utf-8"):
            if line.startswith("#") or line.startswith("config") or not line.strip(): continue
            p = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
            if len(p) < 4: continue
            mm = re.match(r"^(.*?)(\d+)([spdfghik])$", p[0].strip())
            if not mm: continue
            try: E = float(p[3])
            except ValueError: continue
            if E >= lim: continue
            ser[(mm.group(1), mm.group(3), p[1], p[2])].append((int(mm.group(2)), E))
        for key, v in ser.items():
            v = sorted(set(v))
            if len(v) < 3: continue
            d = {n: n - Z*math.sqrt(R/(lim-E)) for n, E in v}
            byn = dict(v)
            for i in range(1, len(v)-1):
                n = v[i][0]
                a, b = v[i-1][0], v[i+1][0]
                if a != n-1 or b != n+1: continue     # only true neighbours
                dl, dh = sorted((d[a], d[b]))
                lo = lim - Z*Z*R/(n-dl)**2
                hi = lim - Z*Z*R/(n-dh)**2
                lo, hi = min(lo, hi), max(lo, hi)
                E = byn[n]
                k = (nm, f"{key[0]}n{key[1]} {key[2]} J={key[3]}")
                res[k][1] += 1
                if lo <= E <= hi: res[k][0] += 1
                else: res[k][2].append((n, E, lo, hi))
    return dict(res)

with State("bracket") as s:
    res = step(s, "run the bracketing test on every channel", run, budget=900)

tot = sum(v[1] for v in res.values())
ok  = sum(v[0] for v in res.values())
print(f"  {len(res)} channels have three or more consecutive members")
print(f"  {tot} interior cells tested")
print(f"  {ok} pass, {tot-ok} FAIL   ({100*ok//tot if tot else 0}%)")
print()
bad = [(k, v) for k, v in res.items() if v[2]]
if bad:
    print(f"  {len(bad)} channels contain a failure:\n")
    print(f"  {'species':<14}{'series':<30}{'pass/test':>11}")
    for k, v in sorted(bad, key=lambda x: x[1][0]/max(x[1][1],1))[:14]:
        print(f"  {k[0]:<14}{k[1][:28]:<30}{f'{v[0]}/{v[1]}':>11}")
else:
    print("  no failures — which would itself be suspect (register 784)")

            try: E = float(p[3])
            except ValueError: continue
            if E >= lim: continue
            ser[(mm.group(1), mm.group(3), p[1], p[2])].append((int(mm.group(2)), E))
        for key, v in ser.items():
            v = sorted(set(v))
            if len(v) < 3: continue
            d = {n: n - Z*math.sqrt(R/(lim-E)) for n, E in v}
            byn = dict(v)
            for i in range(1, len(v)-1):
                n = v[i][0]
                a, b = v[i-1][0], v[i+1][0]
                if a != n-1 or b != n+1: continue     # only true neighbours
                dl, dh = sorted((d[a], d[b]))
                lo = lim - Z*Z*R/(n-dl)**2
                hi = lim - Z*Z*R/(n-dh)**2
                lo, hi = min(lo, hi), max(lo, hi)
                E = byn[n]
                k = (nm, f"{key[0]}n{key[1]} {key[2]} J={key[3]}")
                res[k][1] += 1
                if lo <= E <= hi: res[k][0] += 1
                else: res[k][2].append((n, E, lo, hi))
    return dict(res)

with State("bracket") as s:
    res = step(s, "run the bracketing test on every channel", run, budget=900)

tot = sum(v[1] for v in res.values())
ok  = sum(v[0] for v in res.values())
print(f"  {len(res)} channels have three or more consecutive members")
print(f"  {tot} interior cells tested")
print(f"  {ok} pass, {tot-ok} FAIL   ({100*ok//tot if tot else 0}%)")
print()
bad = [(k, v) for k, v in res.items() if v[2]]
if bad:
    print(f"  {len(bad)} channels contain a failure:\n")
    print(f"  {'species':<14}{'series':<30}{'pass/test':>11}")
    for k, v in sorted(bad, key=lambda x: x[1][0]/max(x[1][1],1))[:14]:
        print(f"  {k[0]:<14}{k[1][:28]:<30}{f'{v[0]}/{v[1]}':>11}")
else:
    print("  no failures — which would itself be suspect (register 784)")
","stderr":""}

them, verify, and only then incorporate.

input.file_text:
# ruled_bracket.py — the sealed bracket (bracket.py, R 796) run under M's ruling
# (RULING-TOLERANCE-489.md, 2026-08-24): STRICT interval membership; the only ε is
# the QUOTATION FLOOR (half a unit in the last quoted decimal of the measured level),
# applied at the interval edges; a cell whose measurement cannot distinguish pass
# from fail is REFUSED, not passed: r = 2*Z^2*R/(nu^3 * sigma) >= 5 (Method §22.5),
# sigma = the quotation floor. Refusals counted separately from pass/fail.
import re, math, sys
from collections import defaultdict
R = 109737.31568

def qfloor(s):
    """Half a unit in the last quoted decimal place of the value as printed."""
    s = s.strip()
    return 0.5 * 10 ** -(len(s.split('.')[1]) if '.' in s else 0)

def run_series(members, lim, Z):
    """members: sorted [(n, E, E_as_printed)]. Returns (passed, failed, refused, detail)."""
    d = {n: n - Z * math.sqrt(R / (lim - E)) for n, E, _ in members}
    byn = {n: (E, s) for n, E, s in members}
    p = f = r = 0; detail = []
    for i in range(1, len(members) - 1):
        n = members[i][0]; a, b = members[i-1][0], members[i+1][0]
        if a != n - 1 or b != n + 1: continue          # only true neighbours (sealed)
        dl, dh = sorted((d[a], d[b]))
        lo = lim - Z*Z*R / (n - dl)**2
        hi = lim - Z*Z*R / (n - dh)**2
        lo, hi = min(lo, hi), max(lo, hi)
        E, s = byn[n]; qf = qfloor(s)
        nu = n - d[n]
        adm = 2 * Z*Z * R / (nu**3 * qf)               # §22.5 admissibility
        if adm < 5:
            r += 1; detail.append((n, 'REFUSED', adm)); continue
        if lo - qf <= E <= hi + qf:                     # strict, edge-guarded by the floor
            p += 1; detail.append((n, 'pass', (lo, hi, E, qf)))
        else:
            f += 1; detail.append((n, 'FAIL', (lo, hi, E, qf)))
    return p, f, r, detail

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # instrument verification on captures/LEVELS-K-I.tsv (the one untested species in the cut)
    lim, Z = 35009.814, 1
    ser = defaultdict(list)
    for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding='utf-8'):
        if line.startswith('#') or not line.strip(): continue
        pp = line.rstrip('\n').split('\t')
        if len(pp) < 4: continue
        mm = re.match(r'^(\d+)([spdfghik])$', pp[0].strip())
        if not mm: continue
        try: E = float(pp[3])
        except ValueError: continue
        if E >= lim: continue
        ser[(mm.group(2), pp[1], pp[2])].append((int(mm.group(1)), E, pp[3]))
    for key, v in sorted(ser.items()):
        v = sorted(v)
        if len(v) < 3: continue
        p, f, r, det = run_series(v, lim, Z)
        print(key, f'pass {p} fail {f} refused {r}')
        for row in det: print('  ', row)

input.file_text:
# run489.py — the ruled bracket over the Spectra Compendium's untested rows.
# Sealed test (bracket.py, R 796) under M's ruling (RULING-TOLERANCE-489.md):
# strict interval membership; quotation floor (half a unit in the last quoted
# decimal of the measured level) as the only edge guard; admissibility
# r = 2*Z^2*R/(nu^3*sigma) >= 5 (Method Section 22.5) with sigma = the quotation
# floor — a cell that cannot distinguish pass from fail is REFUSED. The raw
# tables' unc column is present and NOT used, per the ruling's grounds (R 822, 807).
# Limits and Z: channels.py's LIM (the sealed pipeline's own), cross-checked
# against each row's printed limit; mismatches reported, never silently chosen.
import re, math, glob, os, json, sys
from collections import defaultdict
R = 109737.31568
SP = 'The_Method_1_6___Spectra_Compendium-2.md'

# LIM from the restore point's channels.py (identical to the store's)
src = open('rp/channels.py', encoding='utf-8').read()
i = src.index('LIM = {'); depth, j = 0, i + 6
while True:
    if src[j] == '{': depth += 1
    elif src[j] == '}':
        depth -= 1
        if depth == 0: break
    j += 1
LIM = eval(src[i+6:j+1])

def qfloor(s):
    s = s.strip()
    return 0.5 * 10 ** -(len(s.split('.')[1]) if '.' in s else 0)

def load_raw(name):
